The endangered plant species, Oconee bells, encountered along the proposed transmission line right-of-way, probably would not survive if the trees and shrubs were cleared in its immediate vicinity (Davis, 1955). The Applicant has stated that only tall trees would be cut where necessary, leaving the smaller trees and shrubs (Exhibit W, Appendix G). While Oconee bells withstand transplanting fairly well, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (1976) considers leaving endangered species in their native habitat and protecting that habitat as the better method of preservation.
Clearing should be kept to a minimum, in order to minimize the disturbance to Oconee bells, other endangered, threatened, rare, or uncommon plants that may occur, their habitats, and the vegetation in general. This could be done to the extent practical by locating project facilities in sparsely vegetated areas, and by using such construction techniques as end-hauling of road spoils. The Applicant should avoid the broadcast application of herbicides, except in the most inaccessible portions of the transmission line right-of-way. Selective vegetation control methods should be used to maintain a variety of plants. Cleared or disturbed areas should be revegetated with indigenous plants as soon as possible.
Exotic species should only be considered for revegetation efforts as a last resort. Where selective cutting is not sufficient to allow for transmission line construction, care should be exercised to maintain vegetative soil cover, including existing understory vegetation. Access roads within the right-of-way should be located along topographic contours.
9.2 AQUATIC FAUNA AND WATER QUALITY
Howard Creek is a valuable trout stream and measures should be taken to protect and enhance this resource. Construction of the Bad Creek Project would result in increased sediment loads and reduced flows in Howard Creek. Such effects would reduce the suitability of the stream for trout production for an undetermined period following construction. The Applicant's approach to rehabilitating Howard Creek to preproject conditions appears to be a reasonable plan.
